'''Nhanda''', also rendered '''Nanda''', '''Nhanta''' and '''Nhandi''', is an [[Australian Aboriginal languages|Australian Aboriginal language]] from the [[Mid West (Western Australia)|Midwest region]] of [[Western Australia]], between [[Geraldton]] and the [[Murchison River (Western Australia)|Murchison River]], from the coast to about {{convert|20|km|mile}} inland.  The language is now spoken, or [[Speaker types|semi-spoken]], by only a few people.

The [[Australian Institute of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Studies|AIATSIS]] Austlang database says: "According to [Juliette] Blevins (2001:3) three dialects of Nhanda can be identified: Nhanda, the northernmost dialect, '''Watchandi''' W13, the central dialect, and '''Amangu''' W12, the southern dialect. Thus Nhanda is both a language name and a dialect name". No speakers have been listed in successive tallies since 1975, but the [[Irra Wangga Language Centre]] (formerly Yamaji Language Centre) has been working on its [[language revival|revival]], originally led by Blevins.<ref name=AIATSISw14/> [[Nhanhagardi language|Nanakarti]] was apparently a distinct language.

While Nhanda is usually considered a member of the [[Kartu languages|Kartu branch]] of the [[Pama–Nyungan languages|Pama–Nyungan family]],<ref>Bowern, Claire. 2011. "[http://anggarrgoon.wordpress.com/2011/12/23/how-many-languages-were-spoken-in-australia/ How Many Languages Were Spoken in Australia?]", ''Anggarrgoon: Australian languages on the web'', 23 December 2011 ([http://pamanyungan.sites.yale.edu/master-list-australian-languages-v12 corrected] 6 February 2012)</ref> distinctive features of Nhanda, relative to neighbouring languages have caused some linguists to question this classification,<ref>{{cite journal|last=Blevins|first=Juliette|date=December 1999|title=Nhanta and its position within Pama–Nyungan|journal=Oceanic Linguistics|volume=38|issue=2|pages=297–320|doi=10.2307/3623295|jstor=3623295|publisher=University of Hawai'i Press}}</ref><ref>Bowern & Koch (2004) ''Australian Languages: Classification and the Comparative Method''</ref> and/or classify Nhanda as an [[language isolate|isolate]].

A controversial hypothesis, first raised by historian [[Rupert Gerritsen]], suggests that the unusual features of Nhanda may result from undocumented [[language contact]] during the early modern era, with the [[Dutch language|Dutch]] – in the form of [[Shipwrecks of Western Australia#Timeline of significant wrecks|shipwrecked seafarers]] stranded in Australia before [[History of Australia (1788–1850)|European settlement]] had officially begun.<ref>{{cite book |last=Gerristen |first=Rupert |year=1994 |title=And their ghosts may be heard |location=Fremantle |publisher=Fremantle Arts Centre Press}}</ref> Gerritsen's hypothesis has been rejected by linguist [[Juliette Blevins]],<ref>{{cite journal |last=Blevins |first=Juliette |year=1998 |title=A Dutch influence on Nhanda? Wanyjidaga innga! |journal=Journal of the Australian Institute of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Studies |pages=43–46}}</ref> an authority on Nhanda. Gerritsen critiqued the rejection of his views by Blevins in a subsequent paper, re-outlining his evidence of Dutch influence on Nhanda.<ref>[https://www.yumpu.com/en/document/view/35408141/a-dutch-influence-on-nhanda-rupert-gerritsen-research-and- Dutch influence on Nhanda]</ref>

== Language revival ==
Juliette Blevins, at the time employed at the University of Western Australia, researched Nhanda in the 1990s and early 2000s in collaboration with the Yamaji Language Centre (now the Irra Wangga Language Centre) and published a grammar of the language.<ref name=":0">{{cite book |last1=Blevins |first1=Juliette |title=Nhanda: An aboriginal language of Western Australia |date=2001 |publisher=University of Hawai'i Press |isbn=9780824823757 |location=Honolulu |page=192}}</ref> An  illustrated topical dictionary, ''Nhanda Wangganhaa'', was published by the Yamaji Language Centre in 1998.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Yamaji Language Centre |title=Nhanda Wangganhaa = Talking Nhanda: an illustrated wordlist of the Nhanda language of Western Australia. |date=1998 |publisher=Yamaji Language Centre |isbn=9781875661015 |location=Geraldton, Western Australia |page=62}}</ref> Other published works include papers on its [[phonology]] and history.<ref>{{cite web |title=Midwest Languages: Nhanda |url=http://www.bundiyarra.com.au/index.php?page=mid_west_languages#section4 |access-date=14 January 2020 |website=Bundiyarra Aboriginal Community Aboriginal Corporation}}</ref> Doug Marmion has also been working on the language.<ref name="AIATSISw14" />

==Phonology==
Nhanda differs somewhat from its neighbouring languages in that it has a [[phoneme|phonemic]] [[glottal stop]], is [[initial-dropping]] (i.e. it has lost many initial consonants, leading to vowel-initial words) and the [[stop consonant]]s show a phonemic length contrast.{{citation needed|date=October 2025}}

== Grammar ==
Nhanda is a [[Split ergativity|split-ergative]] language, meaning the nominals take an [[Ergative–absolutive alignment|ergative-absolutive]] case system while the pronominals take a [[Nominative–accusative alignment|nominative-accusative]] one.

Nhanda distinguishes singular (unmarked), dual (-''thada''), and plural forms (-''nu''). The dual suffix is a reduced form of ''wuthada'' ('two'). If a plural suffix is applied to a root that ends with an ''u'', base-final umlaut is triggered and the ''u'' becomes an ''i''. Case and number suffixes have free order.<ref name=":0" />

There are no true unbound third person pronouns in Nhanda.

== Vocabulary ==
{{expand section|date=November 2017}}
The Nhanda word for 'man, human being' is {{lang|nha|arnmanu}}. It appears that when [[Norman Barnett Tindale|Norman Tindale]] collected information on Nhanda (or on the closely related variety thought to have been spoken in [[Geraldton, Western Australia|Geraldton]]) he was given this word, which he recorded as 'Amangu' and believed to be the 'tribal name' for this group. Blevins provides a word list at the end of her grammar.<ref name=":0" />
